item.title: Furniture Plans
item.description:
Plans and references for furniture builds. Add plans here as projects come together.

Pages

  • Cherry Hallway Console (Proposed) — narrow entry console, mortise-and-tenon cherry, drawbored — designed, not yet built
  • Modern Craftsman 2-Drawer Console (Proposed) — 60″ × 16″ × 29″ two-drawer console with lower shelf, proportions taken from the Vermont Woods Studios original — designed, not yet built
  • Heartwood Shaker 3-Drawer Nightstand (Proposed) — 24″ × 18″ × 28″ three-drawer nightstand with arched apron and frame-and-panel sides, proportions taken from the Vermont Furniture Designs original — designed, not yet built
  • Cherry Console + Slide-Under Chest Bench (Proposed) — the hallway console reworked with an open lower half, plus a blanket-chest seat that slides under it and opens fully in place — designed, not yet built

item.title: 3D-Printed Shop Tools
item.description:
Printable jigs and shop tools for woodworking projects — the woodworking counterpart to the rodmaking tool set. This page covers the printed parts that the Adjustable Scarf Jig and the DW745 Mobile Saw Cart plans already call for, plus table-saw accessories that fit any SawStop (they key off the standard ¾″ × ⅜″ miter slot and the flat table, not a model).

All are FDM-printable, generated parametrically, and validated watertight. STLs export in print orientation. Print in PETG (or ASA for the saw-cart parts that live in a hot garage), 4+ perimeters, 40% infill — the ratio gauge at 100%.

Parametric source: generate_woodworking_stls.py — edit the parameter block and re-run (pip install manifold3d trimesh numpy matplotlib). The scarf-jig parts come straight from the plan’s dimensions. The saw-cart parts depend on your saw’s feet, dust port and hose, and the values in the script are estimates — measure yours and regenerate.

Scarf jig

Ratio setting gauge

For: setting the bed’s drop d (= 12″ ÷ ratio) without calipers.

A stepped block whose steps are exactly the drop at the 12″ mark for each ratio, tallest to shortest:

Step Ratio Height
1 1:8 1.500″ (38.1 mm)
2 1:10 1.200″ (30.5 mm)
3 1:12 1.000″ (25.4 mm)
4 1:16 0.750″ (19.1 mm)
5 1:20 0.600″ (15.2 mm)
6 1:23.3 (Rod 002 splice) 0.515″ (13.1 mm)
7 1:24 0.500″ (12.7 mm)
8 1:30 0.400″ (10.2 mm)

Stand it on the bed at the 12″ line and raise the bed until the step for your ratio just touches a straightedge across the rails. It prints on its side so the heights lie in the print plane and come out exact; check them with calipers once after your first print, and adjust the print scale if your printer is off.

ratio_gauge.stl · print 1 · no hardware

Hold-down bar and knobs

For: the plan’s ¾″ × ¾″ × 3″ hold-down across the stock’s top flat.

The bar has two clearance holes 2″ apart, matching an insert pair in the bed (¼-20 inserts, 1″ either side of center), and a shallow pocket for a cork or rubber pad. Print it with the pocket facing up, then flip it over when you fit the pad. Pair it with two fluted knobs, each with a hex pocket that captures a ¼-20 hex-head bolt.

hold_down_bar.stl · print 1 + hold_down_knob.stl · print 2 · hardware: two ¼-20 × 1¼″ hex-head bolts (length to suit your inserts), cork or rubber pad

Pegged fence

For: keeping the stock square to the hinge line without taping a fence on.

A ¼″ × ½″ strip with Ø6 mm pegs that drop into the bed’s ¼-20 inserts on the 2″ pitch, so it registers the same way every time. Print pegs up. Two two-peg segments plus one single-peg end piece cover the five pairs at 7, 9, 11, 13 and 15″ from the pin. The strip is ¼″ thick (the plan’s ⅛″ hardboard fence is thinner) because the peg needs the width; account for that when you set the stock against it.

The hold-down bar uses an insert pair across the bed, so leave that pair’s fence peg out — stop the fence before the bar.

fence_pair.stl · print 2 + fence_single.stl · print 1 · no hardware

DW745 saw cart

These are fit-to-your-hardware starting points. The turnbutton and hook are generic; the foot cup and rear-port adapter use estimated measurements from the plan.

Turnbutton

For: holding the lift-off front skirt panel against its foam gasket.

A 38 × 12 mm rounded tab, 4 mm thick, with a Ø5.4 mm hole for a #10 screw. A quarter turn clamps the panel; turn it back to lift the panel off.

turnbutton.stl · print 6 (plan calls for 4–6) · hardware: #10 × 1″ wood screw each

Wall hook

For: hanging the fence, miter gauge and cord on the cart’s right side.

A J-hook on a 60 × 30 mm plate with two countersunk screw holes. Mount it with the long axis vertical, plate against the wall, so the arm projects out and the lip rises at its end. Print 3.

wall_hook.stl · print 3 · hardware: two #8 flat-head wood screws each

Foot locator cup

For: locating the saw on the support rails by its own weight, replacing the hold-down knobs the skirt would hide.

A Ø40 mm cup, 14 mm deep, on a Ø70 mm flange with two screw holes. The Ø40 mm foot diameter is an estimate — measure the saw’s rubber feet, set FOOT_D in the script, and regenerate. The plan also suggests a TPU liner; print that separately if you want one.

foot_cup.stl · print 4 · hardware: two #8 wood screws each

Rear-port adapter

For: carrying the saw’s rear dust port to a 2½″ hose.

A socket (inside diameter 65.0 mm) that slips over the saw’s port, a short cone, and a ribbed spigot that a 2½″ hose pushes over. The 64.5 mm port diameter is the plan’s measurement from one Type 4 saw — measure yours, set SAW_PORT_OD, and regenerate. Print it upright, socket down.

rear_port_adapter.stl · print 1 · hardware: hose clamp

Table saw (any SawStop)

These are model-agnostic: they use the miter slot (standard ¾″ × ⅜″, 19.05 × 9.5 mm — measure yours to confirm) or the flat table. Nothing here replaces the saw’s guard, riving knife or brake; the push devices are accessories.

Safety. Push blocks and push sticks sit between your hand and the blade. Printed PETG is not rated for that: inspect before each use, discard anything cracked or crazed, never print them in PLA, and keep a commercial push block as a backup. Print the first one and push scrap with the saw off before trusting the shape.

Push block

For: pushing stock past the blade under your hand’s full control.

A heel-and-toe block: a raised grip, a flat base for pressure on the stock, and an 8 mm heel at the back that catches the end of the workpiece so you push it rather than rubbing it. The base underside has a shallow pocket for a ⅛″ rubber pad (spray adhesive). Print it standing on its side (the profile lies flat on the bed); it is solid and fairly heavy, so use 3–4 perimeters and 20–30% infill.

push_block.stl · print 2 · hardware: ⅛″ rubber pad

Push stick

For: narrow rips, where there’s no room for a block between the blade and the fence.

A 250 mm stick with a wide handle (finger hole included), a slim shaft and a 15 mm hook at the tip that catches the back of the stock. Print it flat with the hook pointing up. The hook is only 15 mm deep, so it is for stock about ¾″ and thicker; for thin stock, use a block.

push_stick.stl · print 2 · no hardware

Featherboard (prototype)

For: holding stock against the fence on rips.

Ten fingers leaning 30° toward the feed, on a base with a friction-fit miter-slot runner. This one is a prototype and is friction-only: a plain miter slot has no undercut, so there is nothing for a printed part to lock against, and the runner’s two crush ribs give a light grip. Treat it as a hold-down for light work, not as a kickback preventer, and test-fit it in a scrap slot first — tune RUNNER_CLEAR and CRUSH_RIB in the script until it needs a firm push. If you want a positive lock, bolt the base to a commercial expanding miter bar instead. Print it upside down (runner pointing up) so the fingers stand as vertical walls and flex along their layers.

featherboard.stl · print 1 · no hardware

Setup depth blocks

For: setting blade height or dado depth without a ruler.

Eight steps, ⅛″ to 1″ in ⅛″ increments. Stand a block next to the blade, lay a straightedge across it, and raise the blade until it just touches. Print it on its side so the heights lie in the print plane, and check them with calipers once.

setup_steps.stl · print 1 · no hardware

90° / 45° blade-angle checker

For: a quick check that the blade is square to the table (and at 45°) after you tilt it.

A 100 mm right isosceles triangle, 6 mm thick. Stand a leg on the table and the other against the blade body (between the teeth). The accuracy is only as good as your printer, so check it against a known-good square before relying on it.

angle_checker.stl · print 1 · no hardware

Crosscut-sled runner

For: the miter-slot bars of a crosscut sled.

The tenoning jig uses one of these. A 240 mm segment, 18.6 mm wide (0.45 mm under the slot width) and 8.8 mm tall so it stays below the table surface, with six M5 nut pockets on a 40 mm pitch. Lay the sled base on the runners and screw down through it with M5 flat-head machine screws into the nuts. Print 4 and butt them end to end for two 480 mm runners. A runner this tight is a clearance fit, so tune it with masking tape or thin shims until it slides without side play, and keep the sled’s runners parallel to each other.

sled_runner.stl · print 4 · hardware: 6 M5 nuts and M5 × 25 flat-head screws per segment

Tenoning jig

These print the parts of the Miter-Slot Tenoning Jig; the wood and the clamp are on that page. It also uses one sled runner.

Tenon shim set

For: setting the tenon thickness: s = A − (t + T) ÷ 2, stacked between the fence and the stock.

Five plates — 1/16″, 1/8″, 1/4″, 1/2″ and 1/2″ — laid out on one bed (226 × 222 mm), so any 1/16″ step from 0 to 1-7/16″ is reachable. Print them flat; the thickness is set by layer count, so check each plate with calipers and adjust the print scale or layer height until they match. Each has a pull hole. Print two sets: one for the foot of the fence and one near the clamp.

tenon_shims.stl · print 2 · no hardware

Fence bracket

For: holding the fence square to the base.

A right-angle bracket with a web and two screw holes per flange (Ø4.6 mm, for #8 screws). Screw it into the base and the back of the fence, one at each end. Print it on the base flange.

jig_bracket.stl · print 2 · hardware: four #8 × 1″ wood screws each

Jig handle

For: pushing the jig past the blade.

A flange with two screw holes, a 28 mm post and a rounded top. Screw it to the base behind the fence.

jig_handle.stl · print 1 · hardware: two #8 wood screws

Not yet designed

The plans also call for these printed parts; none of them has an STL yet:

  • Scarf jig: the end-alignment gauge and the beam handles.
  • Table saw: a flip-stop and a sled stop block; a positively locking featherboard.
  • Saw cart: brush retainers, switch bezel, inlet filter frame with sliding shutter, the 4 × 4 × 2½″ wye, manifold collar, collector adapter, cove strips and the cyclone lid.

item.title: DW745 Mobile Saw Cart (Proposed)
item.description:
A proposed build: a small plywood cart on locking casters for a DeWalt DW745 10" jobsite table saw, designed so the saw can live in the garage with as little dust as possible. A jobsite saw’s body is an open frame, with holes on every side and an open bottom. A box under it would only catch what falls straight down, so this cart encloses the saw body on all four sides:

  • a ½" plywood skirt rises from the cart top to a brush seal under the table;
  • everything the saw throws out its sides lands inside the enclosure;
  • a steep V-hopper below feeds a full-width slotted 4" manifold to my Rockler 650 CFM collector;
  • a filtered inlet lets in enough air for the collector to actually pull.

Several fiddly parts are 3D-printed. The saw lifts out after you lift off the front skirt panel.

  • Footprint: 28" W × 24" D. The DW745’s table is about 630 × 570 mm (24.8" × 22.4", per a retailer listing).
  • Saw table height: 34" from the floor, a standard bench height, so a workbench can serve as outfeed.
  • Enclosure: the skirt’s outside is 24" × 21". That’s inside the table’s footprint, so its top edge sits under the table, where a 1" nylon brush seals it. Inside, it’s 23" × 20" for the saw body. The front panel lifts off: its handwheel slot and switch window are open to the top edge, and printed turnbuttons hold it.
  • Below: two ~50° ramps form a V that meets over a slotted 4" PVC manifold. The manifold exits the left side, so the cart can sit against a wall.
  • Storage: a small drawer under the front ramp. The saw’s onboard fence and miter-gauge storage ends up inside the skirt, so hang those on printed hooks on the cart’s right side.
  • Casters: 4 of my step-stop locking casters, plates inset 1", plus ~25 lb of ballast split either side of the manifold.

How the dust gets out

What’s enclosed. The skirt, cart top, hopper and manifold make one sealed volume of about 4½ ft³ gross around and under the saw. The saw’s side vents, bevel slot and open bottom all empty into it.

The saw’s rear port is the best pickup point, right at the blade shroud. Don’t waste it: run a 2½" hose from it out through a grommet in the back skirt panel to a printed 4 × 4 × 2½" wye on the manifold’s exit stub.

Openings in the front skirt. The DW745’s controls are on the front:

  • Handwheel slot. The blade-height handwheel moves along an arc as the blade bevels. Template the arc by taping cardboard over the front of the saw, running the bevel from 0° to 45°, and tracing the shaft’s path. Cut the slot about ½" wider than the shaft and open it to the panel’s top edge, so the panel lifts straight up past the shaft. Close it with two strips of brush seal facing each other in printed retainers.
  • Switch window. A cutout around the paddle switch, also open to the top edge, with a printed bezel and a foam edge.
  • Bevel-lock lever. Check whether it ends up behind the skirt. If it does, extend the window to reach it.

Makeup air: give the collector something to pull

A sealed box starves the collector. With only the throat gap and brush leakage to breathe through (a few square inches), the air would have to squeeze in at over 6,000 ft/min. That costs several inches of water gauge before the hopper, slot and hose take their share, and a small single-stage collector can’t hold its airflow against it. So add a deliberate inlet:

  • Size: at least the duct’s area. Use a 4" × 5" opening (20 in²) high on the left skirt side, near the motor, so incoming air sweeps past the motor and down through the body.
  • Filter: cover it with a MERV 8–11 furnace-filter pad in a printed frame. Air only flows in while the collector runs. When it stops, the filter keeps settled dust from drifting back out.
  • Tuning: the frame takes a sliding printed shutter. Start fully open, and close it partway only if the incense test at the blade throat gets weak.

The numbers.

  • Airflow: the collector is rated at 650 CFM free air. With the inlet, a short hose, and this box, expect 350–450 CFM.
  • Duct and slot speed: that’s 4,000–5,200 ft/min in the 4" duct and about 3,700–4,700 ft/min through the slot.
  • Inlet speed: about 2,500–3,200 ft/min at the inlet.
  • Hose: keep the hose to the collector short (≤ 10 ft) and smooth-walled.

Hopper and manifold.

  • Ramps: two ¼" hardboard ramps run from the edges of the cart-top opening down to the crown of a 4" PVC sewer & drain pipe lying across the bottom at mid-depth. They’re about 50°, well past sawdust’s 35–45° angle of repose.
  • Slot: about 22" long, cut along the pipe’s top between the two ramp feet. Taper it from ½" wide at the exit end to ¾" at the closed end.
  • Ends: the far end of the pipe butts the right side, which caps it.
  • Offcuts: the slot stops larger offcuts, but thin slivers that fall through the throat can still reach a single-stage impeller. Use a zero-clearance throat insert, and consider a cyclone separator ahead of the collector. A printed bucket-lid cyclone works.

Above the table: the part a cabinet can’t catch

For truly minimal garage dust, plan on four more things. The enclosure handles everything below the table, but the top of the blade still throws fine dust toward you.

  1. Over-blade collection. A blade guard with a dust port, or an overarm guard, run on a 2½" line to a second branch on the wye. Check that one fits the DW745 before buying; the stock guard has no port.
  2. A fine filter on the collector. Single-stage bag collectors often pass the finest dust straight back into the room. Check your bag’s micron rating, and upgrade to a 1-micron bag or canister if it’s coarser.
  3. An ambient air filter running during and after cutting.
  4. A respirator for long sessions.

A current-sensing auto switch for the collector is worth it too. The collector starts whenever the saw does, and the motor-cooling rule below takes care of itself.

Measure first

Three measurements set the build. Take them all before cutting:

  1. Body clearance: the saw body’s footprint below the table must fit inside 23" × 20" (the skirt’s inside) through full blade-height and 0–45° bevel travel.
  2. s: from the saw’s feet to the top of the table.
  3. g, measured along each skirt panel’s line. Mark where each of the four panels will stand (24" × 21" outside, centered under the table). At each mark, measure from the saw’s feet up to the underside of the table or fence rail directly above. Don’t measure at the table’s perimeter: the skirt is inboard of it, where the underside can be higher. Each panel gets its own height: g + 1½" − ¼", from the cart top.

Carcass height H = 34" − s − c − 1½", where c is the caster height and 1½" is the support rails.

Example (yours will differ) s c H Interior Ramp angle
3" casters 12" 3.5" 17" 15.5" ~53°
4" casters 12" 4.5" 16" 14.5" ~50°
5" casters 12" 5.5" 15" 13.5" ~47°

The s = 12" and the 11¾" skirt in the example are placeholders. Ramp angle = atan((interior − 4.2") ÷ 8.6").

Brush seal. Use 1″ bristle strip so it bridges uneven gaps and compresses lightly against the table’s underside. Where a panel runs under a telescoping fence rail, leave ~1/16″ between bristle tips and rail so the rails slide freely. The small leak there is just more makeup air.

3D-printed parts

Print these in PETG or ASA, which handle garage heat better than PLA, with TPU where noted for seals and pads. Use 4+ perimeters and 30–40% infill.

STLs (and the parametric source) for the turnbuttons, hooks, foot cups and rear-port adapter are on the 3D-Printed Shop Tools page. Dimensions that depend on your saw are estimates there; measure and regenerate.

Part Qty Replaces / does
Foot locator cups (PETG + TPU liner) 4 Screwed to the support rails, they cradle the saw’s rubber feet. They replace the hold-down knobs, which would be unreachable inside the skirt: the saw drops in, locates itself, and stays put by its own weight.
Turnbuttons 4–6 Hold the lift-off front skirt panel against a foam gasket
Brush retainers 2 Channels that hold the brush strips facing each other along the handwheel slot
Switch bezel 1 Frames the switch window with a foam edge
Inlet filter frame + sliding shutter 1 Holds a 4″ × 5″ MERV pad on the left skirt side
Rear-port adapter 1 Saw rear port (measured ~64.5 mm OD on one Type 4 saw; fit it to yours) to a 2½″ hose
4 × 4 × 2½″ wye 1 On the manifold’s 4.215″ OD stub: main line to the collector, branch from the rear port (plus a second branch for over-blade collection, if added)
Manifold collar (PETG + TPU gasket) 1 Seals the pipe where it passes through the side panel’s U-notch
Collector adapter 0–1 Only if your collector’s inlet isn’t a 4″ hose fit
Cove / fillet strips ~6 ft On the ledge and the rail tops, so dust slides off instead of piling up
Hooks 3 Fence, miter gauge, and cord on the right side
Cyclone lid (optional) 1 Bucket-top separator ahead of the collector

Cut list

Sizes are for the example H = 16″ and an 11¾″ skirt. Adjust the heights to your measurements.

¾″ plywood (one 4×8 sheet):

Part Qty Size Notes
Top 1 28″ × 24″ 21″ × 18″ opening, centered, leaving a 1″ ledge inside the skirt for the support rails
Bottom 1 28″ × 24″ Casters mount here
Sides 2 14.5″ × 24″ Captured between top and bottom. Left side: a 4¼″-wide U-notch up from the bottom edge for the pipe, centered 12″ back from the front (a bored hole would break out of the edge)
Back 1 14.5″ × 26.5″ Between the sides
Front 1 14.5″ × 26.5″ Between the sides. 25″ × 7½″ drawer opening at the bottom
Drawer-bay back 1 ~9.5″ × 26.5″ 6″ behind the front panel. Top edge beveled ~50°
Ramp cleats 4 ¾″ × 1½″ × ~13″ Two per ramp
Saw support rails 2 1½″ × 1½″ × 20″ hardwood Front to back on the 1″ ledges, overhanging the opening by ½″. The foot cups screw on
Drawer box 1 set 24½″ W × 5½″ D × 7″ H From offcuts; slideless, waxed

½″ plywood (a 2×4 handy panel):

Part Qty Size Notes
Skirt front and back 2 24″ × ~11¾″ Front is removable, with the handwheel slot and switch window open to its top edge
Skirt sides 2 20″ × ~11¾″ Between front and back. The left side gets the 4″ × 5″ inlet
Skirt cleats 4 ¾″ × ¾″: 2 at ~24″, 2 at ~21″ Outside the skirt on the cart top, so the inside ledge stays free for the rails

¼″ hardboard (a 4×4 panel):

Part Qty Size Notes
Ramps 2 26.5″ × 13.5″ Edges beveled ~50°. Smooth face up
Drawer bottom 1 23¾″ × 5″

Other:

Part Qty Size Notes
4″ PVC S&D pipe (4.215″ OD) 1 28.75″ Slotted manifold. 26.5″ inside plus 0.75″ through the side plus a 1.5″ stub
MERV 8–11 furnace filter 1 cut to ~5″ × 6″ Inlet pad; replace as it loads

Hardware

Qty Item Use
4 Step-stop locking casters (on hand) Plates inset 1″ from the edges, so the bolts clear the ¾″ walls above
16 5/16″ carriage bolts, 1½″, with washers and nylock nuts Caster plates. Fit them before assembly, heads inside. Counterbore the front ones under the drawer
~9 ft Nylon brush seal strip, 1″ bristle Skirt top edges (~7½ ft) plus the handwheel slot
~4 ft Closed-cell foam weatherstrip Front-panel gasket, switch bezel
1 tube Paintable acrylic caulk or silicone Hopper seams; skirt back and sides to the top
2 × ~12 lb Ballast: a 1″ × 2″ steel bar or a sealed sand tube One each side of the pipe, so the center of gravity stays centered
1 Current-sensing auto switch (recommended) Starts the collector with the saw
~60 1⅝″ and 1¼″ coarse screws Carcass and skirt
— Wood glue, paste wax, drawer pull

Build

The order matters: several parts get sealed in early.

  1. Measure (see above) and adjust the drawings to your saw.
  2. Print the parts above. Test-fit the rear-port adapter and the foot cups on the actual saw.
  3. Bottom panel: bolt the caster plates on, inset 1″, with the heads inside. Counterbore the front pair.
  4. Manifold: cut the tapered slot along the pipe, then cut the U-notch in the left side’s bottom edge.
  5. Box: glue and screw the sides to the bottom. Slide the pipe in through the notch, at mid-depth with its slot facing up, and fit the back. Caulk the pipe to the bottom and to the right side, which caps its end. Fit the printed collar over the notch.
  6. Under the ramps: set one ballast weight on each side of the pipe. Fit the drawer-bay back, then the ramp cleats.
  7. Ramps: glue and screw them on so their feet land on the slot’s edges. Caulk every edge.
  8. Front panel, then the top: caulk the wall tops and ramp heads, then glue and screw on the top.
  9. Support rails and foot cups: set the saw on the rails, mark its feet, and screw the printed cups there. Lift the saw out again.
  10. Skirt, without the saw: fit the back and both sides with their outside cleats, and caulk them to the top from inside now, while you can reach. Cut the inlet in the left side and fit the filter frame.
  11. Front panel: set the saw in its cups, template the handwheel slot and switch window against it, then cut them open to the top edge. Fit the brush retainers, switch bezel, foam gasket and turnbuttons.
  12. Brush seal: fit the brush along each skirt top so the bristles lightly touch the underside, leaving ~1/16″ under the fence rails.
  13. Hoses: connect the rear-port adapter and its hose through the back grommet to the wye, then the wye to the collector.
  14. Test: check with incense that air is pulled in at the throat, the brushes and the inlet. Then run the blade through full bevel and height and confirm nothing rubs.
  15. Drawer and hooks: build the drawer, and fit the printed hooks.

Using it safely

  • Never run the saw with the collector off. The DW745’s motor cools itself with air, and inside the skirt it would recirculate its own heat. The auto switch handles this. Without one, start the collector first and run it 10–15 seconds after the saw stops.
  • Lock all four casters before you turn the saw on. Point the swivels outward as you lock them, which widens the stance.
  • Mind the tipping point. Loaded and ballasted, the cart weighs about 125 lb, with its center of gravity centered by the split ballast. With the casters’ contact about 2¼″ in from the edges, a push of roughly 36 lb front-to-back or 43 lb sideways at table height would tip it. Support long stock with a workbench or roller stand.
  • Removing the saw: unplug it, lift off the front skirt panel (the handwheel and switch pass out through the open slots), and lift the saw out of its foot cups. Do this to clear offcuts from the hopper. Never reach in through the blade opening.
  • Check your collector’s specs. Rockler lists its 650 CFM Dust Right wall-mount (TADC-34WN) as ¾ hp. Measure your inlet and print the adapter to match.

Buy instead?

DeWalt’s DW7451 compact stand is listed for the DW745. It folds and it’s quick, but it has no dust control at all. It’s the better choice if the saw travels a lot. This cart is built for one job: a jobsite saw in a garage with the least dust that a saw like this can practically manage.

item.title: Adjustable Scarf Jig (Proposed)
item.description:
A proposed shop jig for cutting long, accurate scarf bevels in strip stock: the 4½" splice on Rod 002’s bamboo sections, and also scarfed trim, bow and paddle laminations, and anything else that needs a feathered lap joint. It’s a permanent tool, not a one-off. One knob sets any ratio from 1:8 to 1:40, and the setting doesn’t depend on the stock’s thickness.

How it works. Two hard-maple rails form a flat reference plane. A sanding beam rides on them and can’t cut below that plane. Between the rails is a tilting bed hinged so that its top surface pivots on the rail plane. Clamp the stock with its end on the hinge line and drop the far end of the bed. The stock then rises above the rails by exactly the wedge you want removed. Sand until the beam rides the rails, and the bevel feathers out precisely at the end of the stock. The only setting is the ratio: the bed’s drop at the 12″ mark is d = 12″ ÷ ratio, for any thickness of stock.

Drawings

All dimensions are in inches. The X axis runs along the jig, Y across it, and Z up.

Holding the work

A C-clamp won’t work on the bed itself. The bed sits recessed in a 3″ channel between 3″-tall rails, with the base underneath, so a clamp’s lower jaw has nowhere to go. Anything sticking up above the rail plane inside the scarf would also be hit by the beam. The hold comes in three layers instead:

  1. Double-sided tape under the scarf zone (the primary hold). Use thin cloth carpet tape or turner’s tape, along the whole scarf and a few inches past it. It’s the only thing that can hold the feather, the last thin inch that no clamp can reach. On bamboo, press the section down hard for a minute. Release it afterward with a putty knife and a little naphtha.
  2. The hold-down bar goes across the stock’s top flat, knobbed into the nearest insert pair past the beam’s travel. It resists the pull of each stroke. For a scarf of length L, use the first pair beyond L + 3″, and use a short beam (6″ long) on short scarfs so it stops short of the bar. For the 4½″ bamboo splice, that’s the 9″ pair. Pad the bar so it doesn’t mark the enamel side.
  3. The outboard end gets the C-clamp. A rod section is 39″ long and leaves the jig sloping gently downhill (2.5° at 1:23). Support it on a block or roller stand at that height, and C-clamp it there. That’s where a C-clamp is useful: it keeps the long lever arm from rocking the stock on the bed.

Sand with light strokes toward the feather. That pulls the stock toward the hinge, against the tape and the bar, and keeps bamboo fibers from lifting at the thin end.

Settings

Drop d is measured at the 12″ setting mark, from a straightedge laid across the rails down to the bed’s top. Use a depth gauge or the depth rod of your calipers.

Ratio d at 12″ mark Bed angle Max stock thickness (L ≤ 15″)
1:8 1.500″ 7.1° 1.88″
1:10 1.200″ 5.7° 1.50″
1:12 1.000″ 4.8° 1.25″
1:16 0.750″ 3.6° 0.94″
1:20 0.600″ 2.9° 0.75″
1:23.3 (Rod 002 splice) 0.515″ 2.5° 0.64″
1:24 0.500″ 2.4° 0.62″
1:30 0.400″ 1.9° 0.50″
  • Any other ratio: d = 12 ÷ r. For a scarf of length L on stock of thickness t, r = L ÷ t.
  • Capacity: stock up to 2-3/4″ wide. Scarf length L up to 15″, so the maximum thickness is 15 ÷ r.
  • Ratio range: at 1:8 the bed’s far end still clears the base by 0.27″, which sets the steep limit (~1:7.5). Shallow ratios are only limited by how small a d you can measure.

Parts

Part Qty Material Size (T × W × L) Notes
Base 1 ¾″ Baltic birch ¾ × 4-1/2 × 24 Flat; check it on the table saw
Rails 2 Hard maple, quartersawn ¾ × 3 × 24 Glued and screwed to the base edges. Their tops are the reference plane
Bed 1 Hard maple, quartersawn ¾ × 2-15/16 × 16-3/8 16″ from the pin to the far end, plus a 3/8″ nose behind the pin, rounded to a 3/8″ radius about it
Feet 2 Hardwood 1 × 1-1/2 × 4-1/2 Under each end; clearance for the lift knob
Hinge pin 1 ¼″ drill rod (or ¼″ shoulder bolt) Ø¼ × 4-1/2 Through rail, bed, rail at X = 5″, 2-5/8″ above the base’s top. Press fit in the rails, turning fit in the bed
Lift screw 1 ¼″-20 knurled thumb screw, 3-1/2″ — Up through a T-nut in the base at X = 17″, with a jam nut. At d = 0 it stands 2-1/4″ above the base
T-nut 1 ¼″-20 — Base, underside
Bearing pad 1 ½″ brass washer — Epoxied under the bed where the screw tip bears
Threaded inserts 10 ¼″-20 — Five pairs in the bed, at 7, 9, 11, 13 and 15″ from the pin and 1″ either side of center, for the hold-down
Hold-down bar 1 Hard maple (or 3D-printed) ¾ × ¾ × 3 Two ¼″-20 knobs, and a cork or rubber pad on its underside. Sits past the beam’s travel
Fence strip 1 ⅛″ hardboard ⅛ × ½ × 15 Double-sided tape along one edge of the bed; keeps the stock square
Sanding beam 1 ¾″ MDF (or ¼″ aluminum plate on MDF) ¾ × 6 × 10 Wider than the jig, with a handle on top and PSA paper (80 / 120 / 220) underneath
Screws 10 #8 × 1-1/4″ — Rails to base, from underneath

3D-printed parts

A 3D printer makes several of the fiddly parts easier, and repeatable. Print them in PETG, which is tougher than PLA and doesn’t creep under a clamp, at 4+ perimeters and 40% infill.

Part Why print it
Ratio setting gauges A stepped block whose steps are the drop d for 1:8, 1:12, 1:16, 1:20, 1:23.3 and 1:24. Set it on the bed at the 12″ line and raise the bed until the step for your ratio touches a straightedge across the rails. No calipers needed, and the setting repeats. Print it on its side so the steps are accurate, and check them with calipers once.
Hold-down clamps Low-profile cam clamps or bars with a TPU pad, sized to sit under the beam’s path where they can. For narrow stock, a bar with a shallow relief so it presses on the center of the top flat.
Fence strip A thin printed fence with tabs that key into the insert holes, so it registers square to the hinge line every time instead of being taped on.
End-alignment gauge A small block that rests on both rails and drops a lip exactly to the hinge line. Push the stock’s end against the lip, then lift the gauge away. It’s faster and more accurate than sighting with a square.
Beam handles A comfortable handle (and a short-beam version) bolted to the MDF or aluminum beam.

STLs and the parametric source for the ratio gauge, hold-down bar and knobs, and pegged fence are on the 3D-Printed Shop Tools page.

The rails, bed and base should stay wood: their flatness and stiffness are the whole tool. Printed parts only hold, locate and set.

Build

  1. Mill the rails and bed from the same quartersawn board. Plane them to final thickness together so they move together.
  2. Glue and screw the rails to the base’s long edges, with their outside faces flush. Put the screws in from underneath so nothing is near the rail tops. Add the feet.
  3. Drill the hinge together. Shim the bed so its top is flush with the rail tops, and clamp everything. Then drill one ¼″ hole straight through rail, bed, and rail at X = 5″, 3/8″ below the top. That’s 2-5/8″ above the base’s top. Drilling it in one pass is what keeps the bed’s top surface pivoting on the rail plane.
    • The pin goes through the bed. The hole is centered in the bed’s ¾″ thickness, with ¼″ of wood above and below the pin. Leave 3/8″ of bed behind the hole and round that nose to a 3/8″ radius about it. Because the nose is centered on the pin, its highest point stays at the rail plane at every tilt, so it never sticks up into the beam’s path.
    • Fits: the pin is a press fit in the rails. Open the bed’s hole just enough for the bed to turn without play, with a ¼″ reamer or 320 grit wrapped on a dowel. A sloppy 17/64″ hole would let the feather point wander.
  4. Flatten the reference plane. With the bed shimmed flush and clamped, sand the rail tops and the bed top together on a flat surface, such as PSA paper on a jointer bed, a cast-iron wing, or glass. They must be one continuous plane. Check with a straightedge: the bed flush to the rails within 0.002″ is d = 0.
  5. Lift screw: install the T-nut under the base at X = 17″. Epoxy the brass pad under the bed at that spot, and thread in the thumb screw and jam nut.
  6. Marks: scribe the hinge line (X = 5″) and the 12″ setting line (X = 17″) across both rail tops, and ink them.
  7. Hold-down: install the two inserts in the bed, and make the bar and the fence strip.
  8. Sanding beam: flatten the MDF, stick on the PSA paper, and add a handle. Wax the rail tops so the beam glides.

Using it

  1. Zero: with d = 0, a straightedge should lie flat across rails and bed.
  2. Set the ratio: turn the lift screw until d at the 12″ line matches the settings table, then lock the jam nut.
  3. Load the stock: lay it on the bed against the fence, with its end exactly on the hinge line. Sight down the scribed line with a square, then hold it as described in Holding the work.
  4. Sand: take long, light strokes along the jig, starting with 80 grit. Keep the beam flat on both rails. You’re done when the beam rides the rails along the whole scarf and the end has feathered to nothing. Finish with 120 and then 220.
  5. The mating piece gets the same setting and the same procedure. Joined face to face, the two bevels restore the full section.

Accuracy. The pin sits 3/8″ below the bed’s top surface, so the pivot line moves very slightly as the bed tilts. At 1:8 the feather point shifts 0.05″ along the stock and drops 0.003″; at 1:23 it’s about a third of that. That’s well inside the material you trim off the feathered tip anyway.

Rod 002 splice, worked example

  • Joint: 4½″ scarf at the 39″ joint, where the hex measures 0.193″ across the flats.
  • Ratio: r = 4.5 ÷ 0.193 = 1:23.3, so d = 12 ÷ 23.3 = 0.515″.
  • Tip section: lay it flat-side down on the bed with its end on the hinge line. A hex rests stably on a flat, so the bevel runs across the flats. Tape it and hold it down at the far end, then sand with light strokes. Bamboo fibers want to lift at the feather: finish with 220 and keep strokes going toward the feather.
  • Butt section: same setting, same procedure.
  • Mate them: rotate one section 180° about its axis so the bevels face each other. Line up the guide flats, whip the feather ends, and tape the joint, as described on the Rod 002 page.

Variations

  • Router sled for thick stock. A 6″ × 12″ sled spanning the rails can carry a trim router with a flat-bottom bit set flush with the sled’s underside. Run it back and forth along the rails. It’s faster than sanding on 1″+ hardwood. Take conventional (not climb) passes, and use a full hold-down.
  • Longer scarfs: lengthen the rails and bed together. Keep the 12″ setting mark, and capacity grows with the bed.
  • Metric: scribe a second mark 300 mm from the hinge; d = 300 mm ÷ r there.

item.title: Miter-Slot Tenoning Jig (Proposed)
item.description:
A proposed shop jig for cutting the cheeks of tenons on the table saw: the stock stands on its end against a vertical fence, the jig rides in a miter slot, and one pass per face cuts each cheek. Plywood base and fence, a printed runner, shim set and brackets, and a plain C-clamp. It uses only the standard ¾″ × ⅜″ miter slot, so it fits any SawStop (measure your slot to confirm).

How it works. The blade’s distance from the fence is fixed once the jig is set up. Call the distance from the fence face to the blade’s near plane A (1¼″ here). Stack shims between the fence and the stock to move the stock toward the blade. The blade’s near plane then lands at (t + T) ÷ 2 from the stock face, where t is the stock thickness and T is the tenon thickness. Cut, turn the stock end for end, cut again, and the tenon is centered. The only setting is the shim stack: s = A − (t + T) ÷ 2.

This jig cuts the cheeks only. The shoulders are cut afterward on a crosscut sled or miter gauge with a stop, which also frees the waste.

Safety. The stock stands on end with its top well above the blade, so always clamp it — never hold it by hand — and stand to the side of the blade’s plane. Check that the guard or riving knife you are using clears the stock; the cheek kerf is only as deep as the tenon is long, so the riving knife usually runs in the kerf. Run a scrap through with the saw off first.

Drawings

All dimensions in inches. Slot-to-blade distance depends on the saw, so the drawing shows a typical layout; the runner is slotted in the base so you set A once for your saw.

End view looking along the feed

Plan view

Shim table (A = 1¼″)

The shim set is 1/16″, 1/8″, 1/4″, 1/2″ and 1/2″, so every 1/16″ step from 0 to 1-7/16″ is reachable. The stock stands between the fence and the blade, and s is the stack between fence and stock.

Stock t Tenon T s = A − (t + T)/2 Shims
¾″ ¼″ ¾″ ¼ + ½
¾″ ⅜″ 11/16″ 1/16 + ⅛ + ½
¾″ ½″ ⅝″ ⅛ + ½
¾″ ⅝″ 9/16″ 1/16 + ½
1″ ¼″ ⅝″ ⅛ + ½
1″ ⅜″ 9/16″ 1/16 + ½
1″ ½″ ½″ ½
1″ ⅝″ 7/16″ 1/16 + ⅛ + ¼
1½″ ¼″ ⅜″ ⅛ + ¼
1½″ ⅜″ 5/16″ 1/16 + ¼
1½″ ½″ ¼″ ¼
1½″ ⅝″ 3/16″ 1/16 + ⅛

For any other size, s = A − (t + T) ÷ 2, in 1/16″ steps; T = 2 (A − s) − t. If s comes out negative, the stock is too thick for this A — widen A by moving the base (see “Setting A”).

Parts

Wood and hardware

T × W × L.

Part Qty Material Size Notes
Base 1 ¾″ Baltic birch ¾ × 7 × 16 Three cross slots, 7/32″ wide × 1⅜″ long, 3⅛″ apart, centered on the base, over the runner’s nut pockets
Fence 1 ¾″ Baltic birch ¾ × 10 × 16 Glued and screwed to the base’s long edge, standing on it; its face, square to the base, is the reference
Runner 1 Printed 18.6 × 8.8 × 240 mm The crosscut-sled runner from the printed-tools page; nuts in the pockets
Brackets 2 Printed One at each end, on the back of the fence (see below)
Handle 1 Printed Screwed to the base behind the fence
Shims 2 sets Printed One set near the foot of the fence, one near the clamp, so the stock stays parallel
Runner screws 3 M5 × 25 flat-head Down through the base slots into the nuts in the runner
Bracket screws 8 #8 × 1″ wood screws 4 per bracket
Clamp 1 4–6″ C-clamp Fence back to stock face, above the blade

Printed parts

STLs and the parametric source are on the 3D-Printed Shop Tools page: the tenon shim set, the fence brackets, the handle and the sled runner.

Build

  1. Cut the base and fence to size from the same sheet. Cut the three cross slots in the base.
  2. Glue and screw the fence to the base’s long edge, with its face flush to the base edge. Square it to the base with a machinist’s square before the glue sets.
  3. Add the brackets on the back of the fence, one near each end, screwed into both the fence and the base. They hold the fence square under load.
  4. Fit the runner under the base: lay it in the miter slot, set the base on top, and run the M5 screws down through the base slots into the nuts. Leave them just snug.

Setting A (once per saw)

  1. Set the blade’s height to about 1½″ and the jig in the slot with no shims.
  2. Slide the base across (the runner slots allow ±⅜″) until the blade’s near plane is 1¼″ from the fence face. Measure with calipers from the fence face to the near side of the blade.
  3. Tighten the screws. Make a test cut in scrap with a known shim stack, and measure the tenon. Nudge the base if the tenon is off, and note the final A.

Using it

  1. Set the blade height to the tenon length. Use the setup depth blocks to check.
  2. Stack the shims for your stock and tenon sizes (table above) at the foot of the fence and again near the clamp.
  3. Stand the stock on its end against the shims, with the face you want against them. Clamp it with the C-clamp, fence back to stock face, above the blade.
  4. Push the jig past the blade. The kerf is the first cheek.
  5. Turn the stock end for end (180° about its length) so the opposite face is against the shims, clamp, and cut the second cheek. Both cheeks sit the same distance from their faces.
  6. Cut the shoulders on a crosscut sled or miter gauge with a stop block, freeing the waste.
  7. Test the fit in the mortise and adjust the shims by 1/16″ if needed.

Open questions

  • Slot-to-blade distance on your saw determines whether the jig’s base fits left of the blade with A = 1¼″. If your slot is closer, shorten the base; if it is far, the base can be wider.
  • Guard clearance. A crown guard may interfere with tall stock; remove it only if you have a safe alternative.
  • Stock width. The clamp and fence are set for stock up to about 5″ wide; wider stock needs a taller fence.

item.title: Stair Railing (In Progress)
item.description:
An in-progress project: a white oak stair railing built from 4/4 stock, with a flat top rail and plywood art panels hung on hidden cleats between the rails. The drawing set is a 2-page PDF (side elevation + cleat/panel detail); this page is its home while the build comes together.

Drawing set (PDF, 2 pages)

Design at a glance

  • Material: white oak, S3S, 4/4 (posts 8/4); panels are 3/4" plywood
  • Slope: 35.3° (measured), assuming a 7-1/16″ riser and 10″ tread — verify on the actual stair
  • Run: 98″ (8′-2″) along the slope; 80″ clear between posts, 87″ overall including posts
  • Top rail: 1-5/8″ × 3″ (two 4/4 boards face-glued), laid flat; top of rail 36″ above the nosing line
  • Posts: 4×4 (8/4 stock)
  • Infill: 5 panels, 12″ wide, with gaps of 3-1/3″ (all under 4″)
  • Panel mounting: single-4/4 oak cleats (13/16″) hidden behind the panels, set 3/4″ in from the rail’s outside edge so the panel face is flush with the rail edge; the panel butts the rail underside, outside the cleat, and is screwed into the cleat (three 1-5/8″ screws per cleat)
  • Cleat fastening: glued to the rail, plus a 2″ stainless screw every 12″ driven up through the cleat into the rail; the bottom rail is the mirror image (cleat on top)
  • Panel opening: 29-1/64″ vertical between the rails

Notes and open items

  • Test the real art openings against a 4″ sphere — the drawing only checks the 3-1/3″ gaps.
  • Use stainless or coated fasteners with white oak (tannin staining).
  • Panel art in the drawing is a placeholder.
  • Dimensions come from an assumed riser/tread; re-measure before cutting.
